about: A rewrite of the awk text-processing language in Rust, aiming to work the same as GNU awk.

prs.title: An unset variable now equals zero when compared with a number
prs.broken: A variable that was never set was compared as text against a number, so checks like n equals 0 came out false and counters that start empty went wrong.
prs.changed: An unset value now compares as 0 against a number and as empty text against text, as the standard says.
prs.matters: Common awk scripts that count or test variables before setting them give the same answers as gawk.

prs.title: Dividing a built-in variable no longer reads as a pattern
prs.broken: A slash right after a built-in variable like NR or NF started a pattern instead of a division. So NR divided by 2 failed with a syntax error, and some programs printed a wrong number with no error at all.
prs.changed: Built-in variables are now read as values, like any other variable, so the slash after them divides.
prs.matters: Everyday awk arithmetic on line and field counts works as it does in gawk.

prs.title: awk now counts fields right on indented and blank lines
prs.broken: Spaces at the start or end of a line counted as empty extra fields, and a blank line had one field instead of none. Field counts, first and last fields, and rebuilt lines came out wrong.
prs.changed: Spaces at the edges no longer make empty fields, and an empty line has no fields, whatever the separator.
prs.matters: Scripts that read columns from indented or blank lines get the same answers as GNU awk.

prs.title: A bare pattern like /re/ now matches the line
prs.broken: A pattern written on its own, the most common awk program, never matched anything. awk '/b/' printed nothing, and !/a/ printed every line.
prs.changed: A pattern on its own is now checked against the whole line, the same as writing $0 ~ /re/.
prs.matters: Everyday one-line awk filters print the lines GNU awk prints.

prs.title: END sees the right record count and last line
prs.broken: In the END block, the record count was one too high, the last line was empty, an END-only program counted nothing, and the count restarted with each file.
prs.changed: Records are counted only when one is actually read, the count runs across all files, and END-only programs read their input.
prs.matters: Totals and averages printed at the end of a script now match gawk.

prs.title: length without parentheses means the length of the line
prs.broken: A bare length, as in the common one-liner that prints long lines, was rejected as a syntax error.
prs.changed: length with no parentheses is now read as the length of the current line, as POSIX says, and still works inside larger expressions.
prs.matters: Everyday one-liners copied from other awks now run unchanged.

prs.title: Reading a missing array element now creates it
prs.broken: In awk, just reading an array element that does not exist should create it. The Rust awk did not, so counting or looping over such an array found it empty.
prs.changed: Reading a missing element now adds it with an empty value, matching POSIX and gawk. Checking with "in" still adds nothing.
prs.matters: Common scripts that collect keys by reading them, then loop or count, now give the right answer.

prs.title: print now takes more items after a bracketed first one
prs.broken: In the Rust awk, a print line that started with something in brackets, like (x) "-", and then had a comma and more items, stopped with a syntax error.
prs.changed: The comma and the items after it are now read, so these lines print what gawk prints.
prs.matters: Ordinary print lines that start with a bracket no longer stop a script.

prs.title: Big whole numbers print in full, like in gawk
prs.broken: In the Rust awk, whole numbers from 10 quadrillion up printed in scientific form, like 1e+16, and minus zero printed as -0.
prs.changed: Whole numbers now print with all their digits, and minus zero prints as 0.
prs.matters: Scripts that print large counts or sizes give the same output as gawk.
